title: F1 stewards to be more lenient over clashes between drivers in 2026 under expanded racing guidelines
content:
Formula 1 drivers face new standards for the ruling of racing incidents during the 2026 season, after the FIA released its new guidelines for stewards to adjudicate such clashes on the eve of the season opener.

The headline changes cover two particular areas that have become flashpoints in recent years — so-called “racing to the apex” driving and how drivers cannot simply disappear once they have been overtaken.

The changes means attacking drivers will need to be more careful when it comes to making moves for the stewards to rule in their favor in the event of a clash.

The FIA, motorsport’s governing body, has released the 2026 version of the F1 Driving Standards Guidelines (DSG). These are intended to help stewards rule on racing incidents and were first introduced for the 2022 season, following a request for further codification of racing rules by the drivers.

Discussions on the DSG have taken place at the Qatar GP — the penultimate round of the last two seasons — in 2024 and 2025, between the FIA and the Grand Prix Drivers’ Association. All 22 F1 drivers are members of this body.

No major DSG changes were implemented for the 2025 season, though things are different for 2026. One new change states the stewards will now consider if either driver has “released the brakes in order to attempt to gain priority.”

This has been a feature of many racing battles in the last five years, as drivers try to race to get their wheels ahead at a corner apex to claim they have the right then to run another car wide in either attack or defense.

An example of the latter would be Max Verstappen’s defense against Lewis Hamilton when they infamously battled for the lead at Turn 4 at the 2021 Brazilian GP.

When attacking on the inside, a car must always “have its front axle at least alongside the mirror of the other car prior to and at the apex” to be considered to have won a corner, per the DSG. For outside line attacks, the front axle must be “ahead of the front axle of the other car at the apex”.

Stewards will now consider if a driver was attempting to race to apex by releasing the brakes where they would not normally do so, to satisfy the DSG wording.

Drivers must still be in control of their cars and be on a course to stay within track limits to avoid the stewards ruling against them.

But “leniency will be shown where an incident is the result of an attempt to avoid a collision. The guidelines now acknowledge that a temporary loss of control or (tire) lock-up may be due to the ‘laws of physics’ or an attempt to avoid a collision,” per an FIA spokesperson. Tire age and grip level will also be considered.

The 2026 DSG also states that “on long radius curves … the stewards will treat each case on its merits particularly where there is no defined apex or there are multiple apexes”.

This now means that no penalty would be applied to incidents such as Williams driver Carlos Sainz colliding with Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson at the 2025 Dutch GP, which saw the former attempt to overtake on the outside and the latter oversteering into him.

An FIA spokesperson also said the 2026 DSG changes had been made after considering “constructive input of the F1 drivers in Qatar,” in 2025 and “amended to align with the objectives expressed by the drivers and GPDA”.

These additions mean there is now much more scope for the stewards to rule clashes as racing incidents and apply no penalties.

The FIA has also made minor changes to its penalty points guidelines. In 2026, the stewards will no longer impose penalty points “other than for dangerous, reckless or apparently deliberate actions resulting in a collision or for other unacceptable or unsportsmanlike behavior,” according to an FIA spokesperson.

In 2025, any ruling where a driver was found to have caused a collision brought a maximum three-point penalty. This maximum can still be applied if a driver is found to have deliberately collided with another car, but the stewards can now also disqualify a driver if they deliberately collide with another car or suspend them from the next race.

In 2025, Verstappen faced scrutiny in this regard after his apparently deliberate crash with George Russell late in the Spanish GP.

Although Verstappen never publicly admitted the clash was deliberate, he eventually told Dutch broadcaster Viaplay that it was “a mistake from my side” after “all signs went red” in his mind after a previous battle a few laps earlier with Russell and Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc.

In other minor rules changes, drivers will no longer be penalized with penalty points for forcing another off the track during racing battles, but can still get a maximum of three if the action is ruled to be deliberate.
